Amanda, good morning. Thank you for the position sheet. Shall we start with the penalty clause?
Good morning, Henrik. Yes, and I read your comments. Two per cent a week is our number, but I have some room there.
Good. And on liability, we want a cap at the value of the shipment.
That is the one I cannot give you. If we capped our liability at one shipment, a serious quality problem would cost us five times what you could claim.
I understand the logic. But our commercial team will not sign an unlimited number.
Then let us find the middle. If you accept a cap at the annual contract value, we will bring the penalty down to one and a half per cent.
That is interesting. And the dispute section? We asked for arbitration in London.
London is acceptable, but not for free. If I gave you London and the cap on the same day, I would have nothing left to take to my director.
Fair enough. So: London, the annual cap, and one and a half per cent. I will take that to my side.
Agreed, subject to approval. If your team confirms by Friday, we will send the clean version on Monday.

Amanda, this is Henrik, counsel for the buyer. I am sending you our comments before tomorrow so that the call is short. Three points. First, the penalty clause. Two per cent a week is too high for us; if we accept that number, our own insurance premium goes up, and the commercial team will not sign. Second, liability. We would like a cap, and the cap we have in mind is the value of the shipment, not the value of the whole contract. Third, and this one is easier, arbitration. If you agree to London, we agree to the rest of the dispute section as it stands. I want to be honest with you: on the first two we have room to move, on the cap we have very little. See you tomorrow at ten.

Hi Amanda, it is Karin from risk. I looked at the position sheet you sent, and here is where we are before you go into that call. On the penalty, anything above one per cent a week is fine for us, because the insurer covers the difference. On the liability cap, that is the one I worry about. If we cap it at the value of one shipment, a serious quality problem would cost us five times what we could claim, so I would not go there without the finance director. On arbitration, London is acceptable, but do not give it away for free: if they want London, ask for something on the penalty in exchange. And one last thing. If they walk away, we still have the other buyer, so you are not negotiating from a weak position. Good luck tomorrow.

Say what the clause does today, in one sentence. Then say what will happen if the other side signs it as it is. Then say what would happen if the clause came out. Then say which risk your company can live with, and which one it cannot. And finally, propose the exchange: what you can give, and what you want back.
